01 — RESEARCH / MSc DISSERTATION

An answer
is a decision.
So is silence.

Language models can give convincing answers when they are wrong. My research asks whether a model can learn to withhold an answer as its confidence threshold changes.

One LoRA adapter per model. Four reported operating points. A visible trade-off: fewer incorrect responses, but also fewer questions answered.

Read the dissertation ↗

01 / Tune

Learn the threshold.

2,000 unique training questions, eight samples each and a rank-16 LoRA adapter per model. Two epochs, one training seed.

02 / Evaluate

Hold questions out.

500 TriviaQA questions, held out by question text. Greedy decoding, with responses graded by Qwen-2.5-32B.

03 / Inspect

Keep the cost visible.

Accuracy among answered questions sits beside coverage and error across the full set. Abstentions never disappear from the picture.

What these results do — and don’t — tell us
  • Reported in the submitted MSc dissertation, Table 4.4, printed page 27. These experiments have not been independently rerun for this portfolio.
  • All four settings use tuned models. This is a threshold comparison, not a before/after comparison of model training.
  • Thresholds are prompt inputs, not measured probabilities or safety guarantees. The marks are counts derived from rounded reported rates; they do not represent identifiable question-level records.
  • The research reports one held-out split and one training seed. Results were model-graded; agreement was checked against another model rather than human ground truth.
  • Llama and Gemma were tested on TriviaQA only. Mistral was also tested on SimpleQA, where behaviour largely collapsed into abstention. These results do not establish broad generalisation.
